claims.evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Signatures of mitochondria dysfunction were among the very first signs of altered AD proteome.
claims.source: Signatures of mitochondria dysfunction were also among the very first signs of altered AD proteome (Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: Significant changes in regulation of proteins associated with seizures were observed at the transition point between presymptomatic phase and 6 months.
claims.source: Significant changes in regulation of proteins associated with seizures were also observed at the transition point between presymptomatic phase and 6 months which corresponds to the stage where changes in long-term potentiation (LTP) in 3×Tg-AD mice were previously described (Oddo et al., 2003b; Palop et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and citations to published research on LTP changes in 3×Tg-AD mice.

claims.claim: Neurodegeneration-related processes (amyloid load of hippocampus, demyelination of axons and degradation of mitochondria) were noticeably exacerbated with AD progression.
claims.source: Neurodegeneration-related processes (amyloid load of hippocampus, demyelination of axons and degradation of mitochondria) were also noticeably exacerbated with AD progression (Figure 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: Disturbance of the cytoskeleton became prominent only at the late stage of the disorder (18 months).
claims.source: Notably, disturbance of the cytoskeleton, which is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative disorders including AD, became prominent only at the late stage of the disorder (18 months) (Figure 2C) and correlated with the emergence of hyperphosphorylated tau in 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis in Figure 2C and tau phosphorylation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Disturbance of the cytoskeleton correlated with the emergence of hyperphosphorylated tau in 3×Tg-AD mice.
claims.source: Notably, disturbance of the cytoskeleton, which is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative disorders including AD, became prominent only at the late stage of the disorder (18 months) (Figure 2C) and correlated with the emergence of hyperphosphorylated tau in 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and tau phosphorylation data.

claims.claim: Mutant tau, APP and PSEN1 were principally responsible for the differences observed between wild-type and 3×Tg-AD brains.
claims.source: To identify the primary drivers of the phenotypes observed at each stage, identification of top upstream regulators was performed using IPA. This revealed that mutant tau, APP and PSEN1 were principally responsible for the differences observed between wild-type and 3×Tg-AD brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by upstream regulator analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The proteins that are regulated by tau, APP and PSEN1 largely overlap.
claims.source: Interestingly, the proteins that are regulated by tau, APP and PSEN1 in our dataset largely overlap (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Downstream effectors of tau, APP and PSEN1 contribute primarily to apoptosis, mitochondria dysfunction and oxidative stress.
claims.source: Protein enrichment by biological function indicates that these downstream effectors contribute primarily to apoptosis, mitochondria dysfunction and oxidative stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Several proteins involved in mRNA processing (Hnrnpm, Hnrnpl, Nono, Matrin3) were strongly upregulated at the later time points.
claims.source: For instance, several proteins involved in mRNA processing (Hnrnpm, Hnrnpl, Nono, Matrin3) were strongly upregulated at the later time points.
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing increased expression of these proteins.

claims.claim: Expression of mRNA processing proteins increased gradually in coordinated manner throughout the progression of the disorder.
claims.source: Remarkably, expression of these proteins increased gradually in coordinated manner throughout the progression of the disorder (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course expression data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: A group of serine protease inhibitors (Serpina1c, Serpina3k, Mug1) were significantly downregulated by the latest time point examined.
claims.source: A similar coordinated expression pattern was also observed for the group of serine protease inhibitors (Serpina1c, Serpina3k, Mug1) which were significantly downregulated by the latest time point examined (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course expression data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: A reduction in protease inhibitors levels has been linked to aging and cognitive decline.
claims.source: This result is particularly interesting in light of recent findings linking a reduction in protease inhibitors levels to aging and cognitive decline (Castellano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claims.claim: Several inflammation-related proteins (C1qc, Ilf2, Igh-3) and components of myelin sheath (Mag, Mog) were strongly up- or downregulated at the preterminal stage of the disorder (18 months).
claims.source: We have also identified several inflammation-related proteins (C1qc, Ilf2, Igh-3) and components of myelin sheath (Mag, Mog) to be strongly up- or downregulated at the preterminal stage of the disorder (18 months).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomic data at the 18-month time point.

claims.claim: Progressive inflammation and demyelination have been linked to AD.
claims.source: This hints towards progressive inflammation and demyelination in the analyzed 3×Tg-AD model which has been linked to AD (Wyss-Coray and Rogers, 2012; Zhan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on inflammation and demyelination in AD.

claims.claim: Half of the identified putative early markers were previously associated with AD or other neurodegenerative disorders.
claims.source: Noteworthy, half of the identified putative early markers were previously associated with AD or other neurodegenerative disorders (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by literature review summarized in Table 1.

claims.claim: Decreased levels of ApoA1 have been linked to the increased severity of AD in human patients.
claims.source: For example, decreased levels of ApoA1 that we observe in our dataset have been linked to the increased severity of AD in human patients (Merched et al., 2000; Saczynski et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ApoA1 in AD.

claims.claim: Guanosine monophosphate reductase 1 (Gmpr) was identified to be expressed at increased levels in the brains of AD patients.
claims.source: Guanosine monophosphate reductase 1 (Gmpr) which was identified to be expressed at increased levels in the brains of AD patients followed the same direction of change in our dataset (Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Gmpr in AD.

claims.claim: Glyoxalase-1 (Glo1) was previously shown to be upregulated in other mouse models of neurodegeneration.
claims.source: Glyoxalase-1 (Glo1), another protein whose elevated expression was detected in our study, was previously shown to be upregulated in other mouse models of neurodegeneration (Chen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Glo1 in neurodegeneration.

claims.claim: Restoration of Glo1 activity has been proposed as a mechanism to combat cognitive dysfunction in AD.
claims.source: Furthermore, restoration of Glo1 activity has been proposed as a mechanism to combat cognitive dysfunction in AD (More et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Glo1 as a therapeutic target.

claims.claim: Hebp1 was the most highly and consistently upregulated protein at all time points.
claims.source: Among the newly identified putative presymptomatic markers of AD, heme-binding protein 1 (Hebp1) is a particularly interesting candidate. In our dataset, it was the most highly and consistently upregulated protein at all time points.
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing Hebp1 upregulation across all time points.

claims.claim: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family.
claims.source: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family and was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding protoporphyrin IX and heme (Jacob Blackmon et al., 2002; Dias et al., 2006; Taketani et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 protein family and function.

claims.claim: Hebp1 was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding protoporphyrin IX and heme.
claims.source: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family and was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding protoporphyrin IX and heme (Jacob Blackmon et al., 2002; Dias et al., 2006; Taketani et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 function.

claims.claim: Heme is essential for proper mitochondria function and cell survival.
claims.source: Heme is essential for proper mitochondria function and cell survival (Atamna, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on heme function.

claims.claim: Impairments in heme metabolism are associated with AD.
claims.source: Impairments in heme metabolism are also associated with AD (Atamna and Frey, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on heme metabolism in AD.

claims.claim: Cell survival and mitochondria function might be among the first pathways affected in AD.
claims.source: Our data show that cell survival and mitochondria function might be among the first pathways affected in AD (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from pathway analysis data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: An overall increase in expression of both Hebp1 and Glo1 was confirmed in AD patients compared to controls.
claims.source: We could confirm an overall increase in expression of both proteins in AD patients compared to controls that validated our findings obtained in the 3×Tg-AD model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of human postmortem brain samples.

claims.claim: A strong difference in expression of Hebp1 and Glo1 was primarily observed in rapidly-progressing AD cases (death within 4 year period after diagnosis).
claims.source: Interestingly, a strong difference in expression of Hebp1 and Glo1 was primarily observed in rapidly-progressing AD cases (death within 4 year period after diagnosis) (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis and quantification shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: Rapidly-progressing AD cases are characterized by distinct pathological features and clinical parameters and are associated with a faster progression and more severe form of the disease.
claims.source: These cases of AD are characterized by distinct pathological features and clinical parameters and are associated with a faster progression and more severe form of the disease (Chitravas et al., 2011; Zafar et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on rapidly-progressing AD.

claims.claim: HEBP1 mRNA expression in prefrontal and primary visual cortex is significantly elevated in AD patients.
claims.source: The datasets from Harvard Brain Tissue Resource Center (GN326, GN327, GN328) demonstrated significantly increased levels of HEBP1 mRNA in prefrontal and primary visual cortex in AD patients stressing a strong relevance of Hebp1 to AD in humans.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available mRNA expression datasets.

claims.claim: Hebp1 was most abundant in the hippocampus, followed by the brain stem and cortical areas.
claims.source: Immunoblot analyses of four brain areas in 12-month-old mice indicated that Hebp1 was most abundant in the hippocampus, followed by the brain stem and cortical areas (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Hebp1 was not detectable in the cerebellum.
claims.source: Hebp1 was not detectable in the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of brain regions.

claims.claim: Hebp1 became dramatically elevated in all four brain regions in age matched 3×Tg-AD mice.
claims.source: Significantly, Hebp1 became dramatically elevated in all four brain regions in age matched 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed upregulated expression of Hebp1 in neocortex and hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice compared with wild-type controls.
claims.source: Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed upregulated expression of Hebp1 in neocortex and hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice compared with wild-type controls (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Hebp1 is strongly expressed in Ctip2-immunoreactive neurons.
claims.source: Hebp1 is strongly expressed in Ctip2-immunoreactive neurons but is poorly associated with GFAP-stained astrocytes or Iba-1-labeled microglia in the hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Hebp1 is poorly associated with GFAP-stained astrocytes or Iba-1-labeled microglia in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Hebp1 is strongly expressed in Ctip2-immunoreactive neurons but is poorly associated with GFAP-stained astrocytes or Iba-1-labeled microglia in the hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Hebp1 has been proposed to participate in transport of heme from mitochondria to cytosol.
claims.source: Hebp1 has been proposed to participate in transport of heme from mitochondria to cytosol (Jacob Blackmon et al., 2002; Taketani et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 function.

claims.claim: Heme-binding protein 2/SOUL, a homologue of Hebp1, is involved in mediation of cell death by recruitment to mitochondria permeability transition pore.
claims.source: Furthermore, heme-binding protein 2/SOUL, a homologue of Hebp1, is involved in mediation of cell death by recruitment to mitochondria permeability transition pore (Szigeti et al., 2006; Szigeti et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp2/SOUL function.

claims.claim: Subcellular fractionation of the mouse brain indicated that Hebp1 is present in both synaptosomal (P2) and crude mitochondrial (Mt) fractions.
claims.source: Subcellular fractionation of the mouse brain indicated that Hebp1 is present in both synaptosomal (P2) and crude mitochondrial (Mt) fractions where mitochondria are expected to be present (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Hebp1 can be mitochondrially-associated as detected from mitochondria isolated from cultured hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: We further demonstrated that the protein can be mitochondrially-associated by detecting the presence of Hebp1 from mitochondria isolated from cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mitochondria isolation data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: A portion of EGFP-tagged Hebp1 expressed in rat primary neurons appears to be closely juxtaposed to mitochondria.
claims.source: Supporting the biochemical data, we observed that a portion of EGFP-tagged Hebp1 expressed in rat primary neurons appears to be closely juxtaposed to mitochondria (visualized using Mitotracker) (Figure 5C and line scans in Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5C, 5E, and 5F.

claims.claim: The signal from EGFP alone exhibited no correlated association with Mitotracker.
claims.source: In comparison to this, the signal from EGFP alone exhibited no correlated association with Mitotracker (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: The core components of mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), Mic60, Mic19 and Mic25, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
claims.source: Interestingly, the core components of mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), Mic60, Mic19 and Mic25, as well as proteins of outer mitochondria membrane associated with MICOS complex, SAMM50 and Mtx2, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of co-immunoprecipitated proteins.

claims.claim: Proteins of outer mitochondria membrane associated with MICOS complex, SAMM50 and Mtx2, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
claims.source: Interestingly, the core components of mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), Mic60, Mic19 and Mic25, as well as proteins of outer mitochondria membrane associated with MICOS complex, SAMM50 and Mtx2, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of co-immunoprecipitated proteins.

claims.claim: The interaction between Hebp1 with Mic60 was confirmed by immunoblotting.
claims.source: We further confirmed the interaction between Hebp1 with Mic60 by probing the immunoprecipitated complexes with their respective antibodies via immunoblotting (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot validation shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Hebp1 locates in close proximity to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it interacts with MICOS complex potentially through association with outer mitochondria membrane proteins such as SAMM50 or Mtx2.
claims.source: Taken together these data indicate that Hebp1 locates in close proximity to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it interacts with MICOS complex potentially through association with outer mitochondria membrane proteins such as SAMM50 or Mtx2.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing enrichment of MICOS components and outer membrane proteins.

claims.claim: A very similar pattern of subcellular localization was observed in cells that were transfected with full-length Hebp2/SOUL.
claims.source: In line with our observations, a very similar pattern of subcellular localization was observed in cells that were transfected with full-length Hebp2/SOUL (Szigeti et al., 2006), further hinting towards potential role of Hebp1 in the regulation of cell death.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Hebp2/SOUL localization.

claims.claim: Dysregulation of proteins linked to heme metabolism has been reported in AD.
claims.source: Dysregulation of proteins linked to heme metabolism has been reported in AD (Hani Atamna & Frey, 2004; Schipper et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on heme metabolism in AD.

claims.claim: Aβ can form a complex with heme which possesses strong peroxidase and superoxide activities that can contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity during AD.
claims.source: Moreover, Aβ can form a complex with heme which possesses strong peroxidase and superoxide activities that can contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity during AD (Atamna and Boyle, 2006; Chiziane et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Aβ-heme complexes.

claims.claim: Accumulation of Aβ around brain vasculature results in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), microvessel destruction and leakage of free heme into brain tissue.
claims.source: Accumulation of Aβ around brain vasculature results in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), microvessel destruction and leakage of free heme into brain tissue (Chiziane et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on CAA and heme leakage.

claims.claim: High concentrations of free heme are toxic to multiple cell types.
claims.source: Due to its strong hydrophobicity, heme is almost exclusively bound to carrier proteins within cells. High concentrations of free heme are toxic to multiple cell types (Gemelli et al., 2014; Owen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on heme toxicity.

claims.claim: Hebp1 was successfully eliminated in rat hippocampal neurons using CRISPR/Cas9 using three different gRNA sequences.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we successfully eliminated expression of Hebp1 in rat hippocampal neurons using CRISPR/Cas9 using three different gRNA sequences (Figure 7A, KO1-3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing loss of Hebp1 expression in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Treatment of wildtype and control neurons with hemin resulted in 2.69 (±0.15) and 2.86 (±0.23) fold increase in cell death respectively as compared to exposure to vehicle only.
claims.source: Consistent with the cytotoxic effects of high heme levels, treatment of wildtype (WT) and control neurons (LUC) with hemin resulted in 2.69 (±0.15) and 2.86 (±0.23) fold increase in cell death for WT and LUC respectively as compared to exposure to vehicle only (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Hebp1-deficient neurons exhibited no significant cell death in response to hemin treatment.
claims.source: Strikingly, Hebp1-deficient neurons exhibited no significant cell death.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing no increase in cell death in Hebp1-KO neurons.

claims.claim: The protective effect of Hebp1 deficiency against hemin-induced cell death was consistently observed in both gRNA sequences used.
claims.source: This effect was consistently observed in both the gRNA sequences used (Figure 7B, KO1 and KO2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: All 3 groups of neurons exhibited increased levels of cellular toxicity in response to tert-butyl-hydroperoxide or staurosporine.
claims.source: As expected, all 3 groups of neurons exhibited increased levels of cellular toxicity, confirming that loss of Hebp1 is protective towards hemin-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claims.claim: Loss of Hebp1 is protective towards hemin-induced cytotoxicity.
claims.source: As expected, all 3 groups of neurons exhibited increased levels of cellular toxicity, confirming that loss of Hebp1 is protective towards hemin-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of the protective effect to hemin but not other apoptosis inducers.

claims.claim: Endogenous levels of Hebp1 are sufficient to trigger neuronal cell death that is influenced by heme concentrations.
claims.source: These results indicate that endogenous levels of Hebp1 are sufficient to trigger neuronal cell death that is, in turn, influenced by heme concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overexpression did not significantly increase cytotoxicity beyond endogenous levels.

claims.claim: Reduction of Mic60 in cells has been associated with release of Cytochrome C (CytC) and increased sensitivity to apoptosis triggers.
claims.source: In particular, reduction of Mic60 in cells has been associated with release of Cytochrome C (CytC) and increased sensitivity to apoptosis triggers (Yang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Mic60 function.

claims.claim: Release of CytC is often associated with loss of mitochondrial potential and is followed by Apaf1 activation and the ensuing conversion of procaspase 9 into caspase 9 and procaspase 3 into caspase 3.
claims.source: Release of CytC, often associated with loss of mitochondrial potential, is followed by Apaf1 activation and the ensuing conversion of procaspase 9 into caspase 9 and procaspase 3 into caspase 3, thereby committing the cells into apoptosis (Franklin and Robertson, 2007; Zou et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on apoptosis mechanisms.

claims.claim: Exposure of neurons to hemin decreases mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in wildtype, control as well as Hebp1-deficient neurons.
claims.source: Indeed, exposure of neurons to hemin decreases mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in wildtype, control as well as Hebp1-deficient neurons (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial membrane potential assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: A steeper decrease in MMP was observed in Hebp1-deficient neurons (58.7 ± 2.83% and 60.9 ± 1.77% in KO1 and KO2 neurons) as compared to wildtype and control neurons (15.1 ± 2.77% and 14.1 ± 0.22%).
claims.source: However, a steeper decrease in MMP was observed in Hebp1-deficient neurons (58.7 ± 2.83% and 60.9 ± 1.77% in KO1 and KO2 neurons) as compared to the other two groups (15.1 ± 2.77% and 14.1 ± 0.22% in wildtype and control neurons, respectively) strongly suggesting that effects on mitochondrial membrane potential alone cannot be the sole explanation for Hebp1's role in causing neuronal apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial membrane potential assay data.

claims.claim: Effects on mitochondrial membrane potential alone cannot be the sole explanation for Hebp1's role in causing neuronal apoptosis.
claims.source: However, a steeper decrease in MMP was observed in Hebp1-deficient neurons (58.7 ± 2.83% and 60.9 ± 1.77% in KO1 and KO2 neurons) as compared to the other two groups (15.1 ± 2.77% and 14.1 ± 0.22% in wildtype and control neurons, respectively) strongly suggesting that effects on mitochondrial membrane potential alone cannot be the sole explanation for Hebp1's role in causing neuronal apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hebp1-deficient neurons had greater MMP loss but were protected from apoptosis.

claims.claim: CytC was released from mitochondria in all neurons (wildtype, control and Hebp1-deficient) treated with hemin.
claims.source: Indeed, using mitochondria isolated from these neurons, we observe that CytC was released from these organelles in all neurons (wildtype, control and Hebp1-deficient) treated with hemin (Figure 8A and B), confirming that this step of mitochondria-associated apoptosis is not affected by loss of Hebp1 function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claims.claim: CytC release is not affected by loss of Hebp1 function.
claims.source: Indeed, using mitochondria isolated from these neurons, we observe that CytC was released from these organelles in all neurons (wildtype, control and Hebp1-deficient) treated with hemin (Figure 8A and B), confirming that this step of mitochondria-associated apoptosis is not affected by loss of Hebp1 function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis showing CytC release in all neuron types.

claims.claim: Procaspase 9 was cleaved in wildtype and control neurons upon hemin-treatment.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observe that while procaspase 9 was cleaved in wildtype and control neurons upon hemin-treatment, the protein was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Procaspase 9 was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons upon hemin-treatment.
claims.source: Strikingly, we observe that while procaspase 9 was cleaved in wildtype and control neurons upon hemin-treatment, the protein was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Hemin exposure caused a dramatic increase in the population of caspase 3+/7+ cells in wildtype (58.5 ± 2.89%) and control neurons (62.4 ± 1.88%) but not in Hebp1-deficient neurons (8.69 ± 1.55% and 9.86 ± 2.09% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
claims.source: In agreement with this, hemin exposure caused a dramatic increase in the population of caspase 3+/7+ cells in wildtype (58.5 ± 2.89%) and control neurons (62.4 ± 1.88%) but not in Hebp1-deficient neurons (8.69 ± 1.55% and 9.86 ± 2.09% in KO1 and KO2, respectively) (Figure 8D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by caspase 3/7 activity assay data shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claims.claim: Hebp1, found almost exclusively in the mitochondrial fraction in untreated wildtype and control neurons, was released from the mitochondria of these neurons upon exposure to hemin.
claims.source: Noteworthy, Hebp1, found almost exclusively in the mitochondrial fraction in untreated wildtype and control neurons, was released from the mitochondria of these neurons upon exposure to hemin (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Release of mitochondrial Hebp1 in the presence of excessive heme is a critical trigger linking mitochondrial damage to neuronal apoptosis via activation of the procaspase 9 pathway.
claims.source: Collectively, these results indicate that release of mitochondrial Hebp1 in the presence of excessive heme is a critical trigger linking mitochondrial damage to neuronal apoptosis via activation of the procaspase 9 pathway.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing Hebp1 release, lack of caspase 9 activation in Hebp1-deficient neurons, and protection from apoptosis.

claims.claim: Mic60 was released from mitochondria, but only in Hebp1-deficient cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, Mic60 was also released from mitochondria, but only in Hebp1-deficient cells, while Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet for all groups of neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions.

claims.claim: Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet for all groups of neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, Mic60 was also released from mitochondria, but only in Hebp1-deficient cells, while Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet for all groups of neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis showing Cox4 as a mitochondrial marker.

claims.claim: Cytotoxicity was observed in both wildtype (40.2 ± 1.23%) and control neurons (42.8 ± 1.15%) treated with Aβ42.
claims.source: As expected, cytotoxicity was observed in both wildtype (40.2 ± 1.23%) and control neurons (42.8 ± 1.15%) treated with Aβ42 (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Concurrent exposure of wildtype and control neurons to Aβ42 and hemin caused an additional 2-fold increase in cytotoxicity (87.9 ± 1.04% for wildtype and 89.1 ± 0.63% for control neurons).
claims.source: Concurrent exposure of these neurons to Aβ42 and hemin caused an additional 2-fold increase in cytotoxicity (87.9 ± 1.04% for wildtype and 89.1 ± 0.63% for control neurons), an additive effect presumably caused by formation of an Aβ-heme complex that can contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity during AD (Atamna and Boyle, 2006; Chiziane et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data and citations to published research on Aβ-heme complexes.

claims.claim: Very low levels of cytotoxicity were detected when Hebp1-KO neurons were exposed to Aβ42 alone (7.51 ± 0.70% and 7.29 ± 0.96% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
claims.source: In contrast to this, very low levels of cytotoxicity were detected when Hebp1-KO neurons were exposed to Aβ42 alone (7.51 ± 0.70% and 7.29 ± 0.96% in KO1 and KO2, respectively), similar to hemin treatment (9.65 ± 0.77% and 9.42 ± 0.87% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data.

claims.claim: Cytotoxicity levels remained low in Hebp1-KO neurons even after concurrent treatment with Aβ42 and hemin (22.9 ± 0.84% and 23.9 ± 0.84% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
claims.source: Even more significantly, cytotoxicity levels remained low even after concurrent treatment with Aβ42 and hemin (22.9 ± 0.84% and 23.9 ± 0.84% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data.

claims.claim: Hebp1 participates in converging pathways triggered by Aβ42 and heme that cause cytotoxicity via apoptotic cell death in neurons.
claims.source: Thus, Hebp1 participates in converging pathways triggered by Aβ42 and heme that cause cytotoxicity via apoptotic cell death in neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hebp1-deficient neurons are protected from both Aβ42 and hemin-induced cytotoxicity.

claims.claim: Proteins related to cell death, mitochondria function and seizures are among the first affected in AD.
claims.source: Our study indicated that proteins related to cell death, mitochondria function and seizures are among the first affected in AD.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of proteomic data at early time points.

claims.claim: Alterations of cytoskeleton-related proteins became apparent only at the late stage of the disorder which coincides with the timeline of tau aggregation.
claims.source: Alterations of cytoskeleton-related proteins became apparent only at the late stage of the disorder which coincides with the timeline of tau aggregation.

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis of 3×Tg-AD and control mouse brains identified 3760 protein groups, with 2414-2574 proteins quantified at each time point. Principal component analysis revealed that proteins cluster by age (40.9% variance) and disease state (18.3% variance), with increasing divergence between control and AD proteomes during disease progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 are well-supported by the mass spectrometry data and PCA analysis shown in Figures 1C-D. The high Pearson correlation coefficients (>0.96) between replicates (C21) demonstrate data quality and reproducibility. The quantification criteria and statistical analyses are clearly described.

results.result: Age-related segregation in the brain proteome was driven by extracellular matrix proteins and microglia markers, many previously reported as brain aging markers. Disease-related segregation showed APP and tau clustering with AD-upregulated proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by PCA loading analysis (Figure 1E) and citations to prior literature validating these proteins as aging markers. The identification of expected AD-related proteins (APP, tau) provides internal validation of the approach.

results.result: Pathway analysis revealed that cell death, apoptosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction signatures appear at the first symptomatic time point (6 months), while cytoskeletal disturbances emerge only at late stages (18 months), correlating with hyperphosphorylated tau appearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (Figures 2A-C) and tau phosphorylation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The temporal progression of pathway changes is clearly documented, though the mechanistic connections between pathways remain correlative rather than causal.

results.result: Upstream regulator analysis identified mutant tau, APP, and PSEN1 as principal drivers of differences between wild-type and 3×Tg-AD brains, with their downstream effectors largely overlapping and contributing primarily to apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by IPA upstream regulator analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C). The overlap analysis and functional enrichment provide mechanistic insights, though these are computational predictions based on literature knowledge rather than direct experimental validation.

results.result: Several protein groups showed coordinated temporal expression changes during AD progression, including mRNA processing proteins (Hnrnpm, Hnrnpl, Nono, Matrin3) that were progressively upregulated and serine protease inhibitors (Serpina1c, Serpina3k, Mug1) that were progressively downregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by time-course expression data (Figures 2H-I). The coordinated expression patterns suggest functional relationships, though the biological significance requires further investigation. The connection to cognitive decline (C39) is supported by citation but not directly tested.

results.result: Hebp1 was identified as the most highly and consistently upregulated protein at all time points in 3×Tg-AD mice, including the presymptomatic stage (2 months).
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C111 are directly supported by the proteomic data showing Hebp1 upregulation across all time points (Figures 2J-L). The consistency of upregulation and early appearance make Hebp1 a strong candidate presymptomatic marker.

results.result: Hebp1 and Glo1 expression was elevated in human AD patients compared to controls, with the strongest differences observed in rapidly-progressing AD cases (death within 4 years of diagnosis).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 and C112 are supported by immunoblot analysis of human postmortem brain samples (Figures 3A-C). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.025 for Hebp1, p<0.001 for Glo1 in rpAD vs control). However, sample sizes are modest (n=8-9 per group) and the rapidly-progressing classification relies on retrospective clinical assessment.

results.result: Analysis of publicly available datasets demonstrated significantly elevated HEBP1 mRNA expression in prefrontal and primary visual cortex of AD patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by analysis of Harvard Brain Tissue Resource Center datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing statistically significant increases (p<0.0001) in multiple brain regions. The large sample sizes (n=133-417) strengthen these findings, though the effect sizes appear modest.

results.result: Hebp1 showed region-specific expression in mouse brain, being most abundant in hippocampus, followed by brain stem and cortex, but undetectable in cerebellum. Expression was dramatically elevated in all four regions in 3×Tg-AD mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by immunoblot analysis (Figure 4A) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The regional distribution and disease-related upregulation are clearly demonstrated, though quantification of the immunohistochemistry would strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Hebp1 is predominantly expressed in Ctip2-positive neurons but shows poor association with GFAP-positive astrocytes or Iba-1-positive microglia in the hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C61-C62 are supported by co-immunostaining data (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The cell-type specificity is clearly demonstrated through colocalization analysis with multiple cell-type markers. This neuronal localization is important for understanding Hebp1's role in AD pathology.

results.result: Hebp1 exhibits perimitochondrial localization, as demonstrated by subcellular fractionation showing presence in synaptosomal and crude mitochondrial fractions, detection in isolated mitochondria from cultured neurons, and live imaging showing EGFP-Hebp1 juxtaposed to mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C65-C68 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: subcellular fractionation (Figure 5A), mitochondria isolation (Figure 5B), and live imaging (Figures 5C-F). The convergence of biochemical and imaging evidence strongly supports the perimitochondrial localization, though the protein lacks a canonical mitochondrial targeting sequence.

results.result: Hebp1 interacts with the mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), with core components Mic60, Mic19, and Mic25, as well as outer membrane proteins SAMM50 and Mtx2, enriched in Hebp1 co-immunoprecipitation samples. The Hebp1-Mic60 interaction was confirmed by immunoblotting.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C69-C72 are supported by co-IP mass spectrometry (Figure 6A) and immunoblot validation (Figure 6B). The identification of multiple MICOS components and associated proteins provides strong evidence for this interaction. However, the stoichiometry and functional significance of these interactions require further investigation.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of Hebp1 in rat hippocampal neurons protected against hemin-induced cytotoxicity. Wildtype neurons showed 2.69-2.86 fold increase in cell death upon hemin treatment, while Hebp1-deficient neurons exhibited no significant cell death, with this protective effect consistently observed across multiple gRNA sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C78-C81 are supported by CRISPR knockout validation (Figure 7A) and cytotoxicity assays (Figure 7B). The use of multiple independent gRNAs (KO1, KO2) strengthens the conclusion that the protective effect is specifically due to Hebp1 loss. Statistical significance is clearly demonstrated (p<0.001).

results.result: The protective effect of Hebp1 deficiency was specific to hemin-induced cytotoxicity, as all neuron groups (wildtype, control, and Hebp1-deficient) showed increased toxicity in response to tert-butyl-hydroperoxide or staurosporine.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are supported by cytotoxicity assays with alternative apoptosis inducers (Figures 7C-D). This specificity control is critical for establishing that Hebp1's role is specifically related to heme-mediated toxicity rather than general apoptosis resistance.

results.result: Hemin treatment decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in all neuron types, but Hebp1-deficient neurons showed a steeper decrease (58.7-60.9%) compared to wildtype and control neurons (14.1-15.1%), suggesting that mitochondrial membrane potential changes alone cannot explain Hebp1's role in neuronal apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by mitochondrial membrane potential assays (Figure 7E). The paradoxical finding that Hebp1-deficient neurons have greater MMP loss but are protected from apoptosis is well-documented and appropriately interpreted as evidence that Hebp1 acts downstream of or independently from MMP changes.

results.result: Cytochrome C was released from mitochondria in all neuron types upon hemin treatment, but procaspase 9 activation occurred only in wildtype and control neurons, not in Hebp1-deficient neurons, indicating that Hebp1 deficiency blocks the mitochondrial-associated caspase signaling pathway downstream of CytC release.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C90-C93 are supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions (Figures 8A-C). The demonstration that CytC release occurs normally but caspase 9 activation is blocked in Hebp1-deficient neurons identifies a specific mechanistic step where Hebp1 functions. This is a key finding for understanding the apoptotic pathway.

results.result: Hemin exposure caused dramatic increases in caspase 3/7+ cells in wildtype (58.5%) and control neurons (62.4%) but not in Hebp1-deficient neurons (8.69-9.86%). Hebp1 was released from mitochondria upon hemin exposure, suggesting that mitochondrial Hebp1 release is a critical trigger linking mitochondrial damage to neuronal apoptosis via procaspase 9 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by caspase 3/7 activity assays (Figures 8D-E) and subcellular fractionation (Figure 8B). The correlation between Hebp1 release and caspase activation is compelling, though the mechanistic details of how Hebp1 promotes caspase 9 activation remain unclear. The inference in C96 is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: Hebp1-deficient neurons were protected from Aβ42-induced cytotoxicity (7.29-7.51% vs 40.2-42.8% in controls) and showed minimal cytotoxicity even with concurrent Aβ42 and hemin treatment (22.9-23.9% vs 87.9-89.1% in controls), indicating that Hebp1 participates in converging pathways triggered by Aβ42 and heme.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by cytotoxicity assays with Aβ42 alone and in combination with hemin (Figure 9). The protection against Aβ42 toxicity extends Hebp1's relevance beyond heme-specific effects to broader AD pathology. However, the mechanism by which Hebp1 mediates Aβ42 toxicity requires further investigation.

results.result: Mic60 was released from mitochondria specifically in Hebp1-deficient cells upon hemin treatment, while Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet across all neuron types.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are supported by immunoblot analysis of subcellular fractions (Figure 8A-B). The selective release of Mic60 in Hebp1-deficient neurons is an intriguing observation, though the authors appropriately note that its significance remains unclear. This finding warrants further investigation.

results.result: Background claims establishing AD as the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by Aβ plaques and tau tangles, affecting >40 million people worldwide, with mutations in APP and presenilins causing familial AD, though Aβ and tau aggregation alone do not fully account for cognitive decline.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C16 represent established knowledge about AD pathology and epidemiology, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: The 3×Tg-AD mouse model harbors three mutated genes (PSEN1 M146V, APP Swe, MAPT P301L) and develops AD-related phenotypes progressively, mimicking the human disorder.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 describe the mouse model used in the study, supported by citations to the original publications characterizing this model. This is standard methodological information rather than a novel finding.

results.result: Half of the identified presymptomatic markers were previously associated with AD or other neurodegenerative disorders, including ApoA1, Gmpr, and Glo1, with Glo1 restoration proposed as a therapeutic mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by literature review (Table 1) and appropriate citations. This validation against prior literature strengthens confidence in the proteomic approach, though these are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family and was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding heme. Heme is essential for mitochondrial function and cell survival, with impairments in heme metabolism associated with AD. Hebp1 has been proposed to transport heme from mitochondria to cytosol, and its homolog Hebp2/SOUL mediates cell death through mitochondrial permeability transition pore recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51, C63-C64 represent prior knowledge about Hebp1 and related proteins, supported by appropriate citations. This background information provides important context for interpreting the novel findings but is not original to this study.

results.result: Cell survival, mitochondrial function, and seizure-related proteins are among the first pathways affected in AD based on proteomic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C104 are supported by pathway analysis (Figures 2A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). This represents an important finding about early AD pathology, though the inference is based on correlative proteomic changes rather than direct functional evidence.

results.result: Cytoskeleton-related protein alterations became apparent only at late disease stages, coinciding with tau aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by pathway analysis and tau phosphorylation data. This temporal relationship between cytoskeletal changes and tau pathology is well-documented and provides insight into disease progression.

results.result: mRNA processing proteins including Matrin-3, Nono, Hnrnpm, and Hnrnpl showed progressive upregulation during AD, with U1 snRNP components previously found enriched in insoluble brain proteome of AD patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by proteomic data and citations to prior literature. The coordinated upregulation of mRNA processing proteins suggests dysregulation of this process in AD, though functional validation is needed.

results.result: Serpins were downregulated in both this study and a 5×FAD mouse model, with protease inhibitor restoration (e.g., TIMP2) shown to improve cognitive function in aged mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are supported by citations to prior studies. The convergence of findings across different AD models strengthens the relevance of serpin downregulation, though this is confirmatory rather than novel.

results.result: Rapidly-progressing AD cases are characterized by distinct pathological features and clinical parameters, associated with faster progression and more severe disease.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing rapidly-progressing AD. This provides important context for interpreting the differential Hebp1 expression in these patients.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that Hebp2/SOUL shows similar subcellular localization to Hebp1, heme metabolism is dysregulated in AD, Aβ-heme complexes contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity, cerebral amyloid angiopathy leads to heme leakage, and free heme is toxic to cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 represent prior knowledge supported by appropriate citations. This background establishes the biological plausibility of Hebp1's role in AD pathology through heme-mediated mechanisms.

results.result: Endogenous Hebp1 levels are sufficient to trigger neuronal cell death influenced by heme concentrations, as overexpression did not significantly increase cytotoxicity beyond endogenous levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by overexpression data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showing that increased hemin concentration, rather than Hebp1 overexpression, drives cytotoxicity. This suggests Hebp1 functions in a heme-dependent manner at physiological expression levels.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that Mic60 reduction increases apoptosis through CytC release, CytC release leads to caspase 9 and 3 activation, SOUL promotes cell death through mitochondrial membrane permeabilization, neuronal loss in AD is attributed to apoptosis, and anti-apoptotic interventions decrease pathology in 3×Tg-AD mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C113-C117 represent established knowledge about apoptotic pathways and their relevance to AD, supported by appropriate citations. This provides the mechanistic framework for interpreting Hebp1's role in the caspase cascade.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that heme oxygenase-1 reduces Aβ-induced cytotoxicity, heme synthesis is impaired in AD with potential heme overload, cerebral amyloid angiopathy contributes to AD and causes vascular disruption with heme release, and CAA is associated with apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C123 represent prior knowledge supported by citations, establishing multiple potential sources of heme dysregulation in AD and connecting vascular pathology to heme-mediated neurotoxicity.

results.result: Cathepsin D cleaves Hebp1 to generate F2L peptide that binds FPR2 on microglia and promotes migration. FPR2-positive microglia are recruited to Aβ plaques in AD patients. Cathepsin D expression correlates with aging in the dataset and is increased in AD patient hippocampus, suggesting possible F2L-mediated microglial recruitment during AD.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 are supported by citations and proteomic data showing cathepsin D upregulation. However, C129 is speculative, as the authors appropriately note with "it is possible that." No direct evidence is provided for F2L generation or microglial recruitment in their experimental system. This represents an interesting hypothesis requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Hebp1 plays a role in progressive neuronal loss during AD progression.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 represents the overall conclusion of the study, supported by the combined evidence of Hebp1 upregulation in AD (C2, C47, C53-C54), neuronal expression (C3, C61-C62), mitochondrial localization (C5, C65-C68), MICOS interaction (C4, C69-C72), and mediation of heme- and Aβ-induced apoptosis (C6-C8, C78-C103). While the in vitro mechanistic studies are compelling, direct demonstration of Hebp1's role in neuronal loss in vivo would strengthen this conclusion.
